gabapentin|egfr<30:
Gabapentin is cleared almost entirely by the kidneys without being metabolized, so its dose is generally scaled to estimated creatinine clearance or eGFR. Labeling and clinical references describe progressively lower total daily doses and longer dosing intervals as kidney function declines (commonly using bands such as roughly 30 to 59, 15 to 29, and below 15 mL/min), with supplemental dosing after hemodialysis. In reduced kidney function, the drug accumulates, and reported effects of excess exposure include sedation, dizziness, confusion, unsteadiness, and in some cases myoclonus or other neurologic toxicity, so monitoring in these groups typically centers on these symptoms and on repeat kidney function checks, since eGFR can change over time.

In people with normal kidney function, the standard labeled dose ranges apply, and monitoring is mainly clinical, looking at response and side effects such as drowsiness, dizziness, and swelling. Gabapentin absorption is also saturable, meaning higher single doses are absorbed proportionally less, which is one reason it is usually divided across the day.

For people with high or supranormal clearance, there is little formal dosing guidance, and no established adjustment recommendations exist for eGFR above the normal range. Because clearance is higher, drug levels may be lower for a given dose, but how much this matters clinically is not well defined, and dosing in this group generally relies on the standard range and observed response.

Older adults often have lower kidney function than creatinine alone suggests, which is why clearance estimates are emphasized in this group. A pharmacist can help check which kidney function estimate and dosing band apply to a specific prescription.
lithium|sodium<135:
Lithium is handled by the kidneys in much the same way as sodium, so the serum sodium level and overall salt and water balance influence how much lithium the body retains. When sodium is low (from salt restriction, vomiting, diarrhea, sweating, or certain diuretics), the kidneys reabsorb more lithium and blood levels can rise, which is why clinicians often check lithium concentrations more closely and may lower the dose during these periods. When sodium is normal and stable, lithium is typically monitored at routine intervals, along with kidney and thyroid function, with the dose adjusted to keep the serum lithium within a target range set by the prescriber. When sodium is high, usually from dehydration or conditions such as diabetes insipidus (which lithium itself can cause), lithium handling and kidney function can be affected in ways that vary, so the cause of the high sodium and the lithium level are generally reviewed together.

Across all ranges, there is no single universal dosing formula tied to specific sodium values, and adjustments are individualized by the prescriber based on repeat lithium levels, symptoms, kidney function, and the cause of the sodium change. A pharmacist can help explain which situations, such as illness with fluid loss or changes in diet or other medicines, usually prompt a closer look at lithium levels.
methotrexate|egfr<60: Methotrexate is cleared mostly by the kidneys, so lower eGFR raises drug exposure and the risk of bone marrow suppression, mucositis, liver injury and lung toxicity. In general, guidance describes more frequent blood monitoring (blood counts, kidney and liver tests) and lower doses as eGFR falls, with many references advising caution at moderate impairment (roughly eGFR 30 to 59) and avoidance of use or very restricted use below about 30, though exact cutoffs and dose reductions differ between sources and indications. With normal kidney function, routine monitoring still applies, typically blood counts, creatinine/eGFR and liver tests at regular intervals, because kidney function can change with illness, dehydration, or other medicines that reduce methotrexate clearance. For high or supranormal eGFR, there is no well-established dosing adjustment, and little evidence on whether faster clearance meaningfully reduces effectiveness, so standard dosing and monitoring are generally used. Because thresholds and schedules vary by guideline, dose (low-dose weekly versus high-dose oncology use) and individual factors, a pharmacist or prescriber can explain which approach applies to a specific situation.
simvastatin|alt>120: For people with normal ALT, labeling generally recommends a baseline liver enzyme check before starting simvastatin and a repeat only if symptoms or clinical concerns arise, since routine periodic monitoring is no longer advised. Low ALT is not a recognized reason to adjust simvastatin and has no established monitoring implications. Mildly elevated ALT (up to about 3 times the upper limit of normal) is common in fatty liver disease, and statins are generally not considered contraindicated in that range, though clinicians often recheck levels to see whether they hold steady. Persistently elevated ALT above 3 times the upper limit, or unexplained elevations at any level, has historically led to dose reduction or discontinuation, and active liver disease or unexplained persistent transaminase elevation is listed as a labeled contraindication. Because the specific thresholds, retesting schedule, and dose decisions depend on the cause of the elevation and the individual's overall picture, these are matters a pharmacist or prescriber would need to weigh case by case.

valproate|alt>120: Valproate can raise liver enzymes, and mild, often transient ALT elevations occur in a sizable minority of people taking it, so monitoring is generally recommended, especially in the first six months and in people with other risk factors for liver injury. There is no universally agreed ALT cutoff or adjustment schedule; guidance comes mainly from product labeling and expert consensus, and the practical approach varies between prescribers and countries. In general, normal or low ALT is treated as a baseline to compare against, mildly raised values (often under about 2 to 3 times the upper limit of normal) are commonly followed with repeat testing rather than immediate change, and markedly raised values or any elevation accompanied by symptoms such as persistent nausea, vomiting, jaundice, unusual fatigue, or loss of seizure control are treated as a possible sign of serious liver injury that needs prompt medical evaluation. Rare but severe liver failure is the main concern, with higher risk reported in young children, those on multiple anti-seizure drugs, and people with certain metabolic or mitochondrial disorders, and ALT alone does not reliably predict it. Because decisions depend on the size and trend of the rise, symptoms, and the reason valproate is being used, a pharmacist or prescriber would need to interpret the specific numbers.
